title: How Milt Hinton got the nickname 'Judge'
summary: Leeman asks and Hinton explains that his nickname began when he arrived early at studios and greeted everyone, echoing his grandmother's story of a jailed man and the judge.

story.theme_name: How I got my name: nicknames and band monikers
story.community_name: How I got my name: nicknames and band names

blocks.x: This is Saturday, March 3rd, and this is the 8th day that we're under these tapes, Milt Hinton. Milton, it just dawned on me that for many, many years, I've always called you 'Judge' -- that's been your nickname and every musician I know has always called you Judge over the years. I haven't used that expression -- while you've been my interviewer and on these tapes and so forth, and I always took it for granted that when any of us had problems or were in trouble or anything, we always respected your opinion and we asked you as a friend what you thought about our situations, and we always relied upon your answers as very helpful, and your decisions were final, so possibly that's where the expression, 'the judge' came from?
And I think that since you are my interviewer on these tapes, that you should tell the people how come you were named the judge.

Hey, Cliff, it's funny you should ask that, for me to explain how I got the nickname "Judge." But it certainly didn't have anything to do with my judiciary or my tremendous knowledge anymore than any other person. It just so happened that many years ago in the recording studios, when I first broke into the studios, you know how it's necessary to be punctual and on time and everything. I always tried to be on time and be one of the first ones in the studio so I could get my instrument out and tune up and be ready to play.

It reminded me of an old story that my grandmother used to tell about a dear soul brother in Mississippi where my grandmother came from, that was just a beautiful soul. Everybody in town loved him, but he always had a way of getting in his cups, and on weekends, Saturday night he decided that he should get drunk. Everybody loved him. He worked all the week and every Saturday night this fellow got drunk and he's laying out in the streets on the corners and he's very inebriated and very happy, talking a little loud. So, late Saturday night the police would come along and they didn't want him to be seen on the corner laying in the streets when people got ready to go to church Sunday morning. Late Saturday night they used to lock him up and put him in jail for safe-keeping over Sunday---let him sleep it off. And Monday morning when court opened they'd let him out and he was always the first one in court. When he came the judge would be sitting there all clean and everything and he'd say: "Would you please get out of,here!"

And I think I told this story many years ago and in the morning when I walked in a recording studio, when everybody came in I would say, "Good morning, Judge." And that's actually the way the name got started. Not the brilliance of----Naturally, over the years I've become one of the senior citizens of the recording business. Being an older person they'll say, "Well, here comes the Judge and we'll ask him what he thinks about that."

But that's honestly. It's wonderful to hear you tell these stories about these great Gibson parties and the different parties in Odessa and Midland. And you know, Cliff, that I have been on some of these parties, not as many as you have, and I have been the recipient of those sheriff badges, not as many as you, and ten-gallon hat and silver buckle. And I'm very grateful to have them along with you. You've made me responsible for being on those parties and I just want to thank you for that. Will you please continue with your story.
